> **Proposed API.** This guide follows `docs/api-vision.md`, not the current
> implementation. All code is static and has not been run. Provider examples
> would need credentials and may create, change, retrieve or delete remote work.
> Any displayed status below is an illustration, not a captured result.

A file description is a value. A batch job is remote work. A live session is
an open connection. They should not look interchangeable merely because all
three are represented by R objects.

The proposed API makes one question easy to answer at each step:
**am I reading a local snapshot, or asking for an operation?**

```r
library(lm15)
```

## Describe the upload, then upload it

```r
client <- new_lm(
  "anthropic",
  credential = credential_env("ANTHROPIC_API_KEY")
)

upload <- file_upload_request(
  "notes.txt",
  bytes_data = charToRaw("These are the meeting notes."),
  media_type = "text/plain"
)
```

The client is a recipe, and `upload` is a value. No credential has been read
and no file has been sent.

```r
file <- file_upload(client, upload)
file$id
```

`file_upload()` performs the operation. The returned file information is a
snapshot of what the provider reported; reading `file$id` does not refresh it.
An ID is not the same thing as local bytes or guaranteed download permission.

The existing explicit resource names remain:

```r
current_file <- file_get(client, file$id)
page <- file_list(client)
file_delete(client, file$id)
```

Each line asks the provider to do work. The last deletes the remote file.
There is no automatic deletion because an R variable went out of scope, and
no hidden download when a field is printed.

## A batch contains complete requests

```r
submission <- batch_request(list(
  request("claude-sonnet-4-6", message_user("Say hello.")),
  request("claude-sonnet-4-6", message_user("Say goodbye."))
))

job <- batch(client, submission)
job
```

A possible proposed structural display is:

```text
<lm15 batch job [shared resource]>
  cached status: running
  snapshot() is local; refresh() fetches status
```

The example does not predict how quickly a provider will start or finish a
job. A submission can require provider-specific preparation, but `batch()`
must not poll until completion as an undocumented side effect.

A provider-specific client takes that provider's model IDs. The router's
`provider:model` prefix belongs to routing, not to these already-bound requests.

## Keep snapshots separate from shared handles

```r
before <- snapshot(job)
also_job <- job

refresh(job)
after <- snapshot(job)
```

`before` and `after` are independent values. The handle is a shared resource:
`also_job` and `job` observe the same updated cached status. The proposed
`refresh()` performs one provider status fetch, updates that shared handle,
and returns it invisibly. Credential resolution may do additional preparatory
work, but the operation does not repeatedly poll.

`snapshot()` never contacts the provider. Existing `job_info(job)` remains a
compatibility spelling for this local job operation, not a second recommended
snapshot API. Callers should not need to inspect or edit a public `$state`
environment.

## Only `wait()` polls a job

```r
job <- wait(
  job,
  timeout = 60,
  poll_every = 5,
  control = request_control(connect_timeout = 10)
)
info <- snapshot(job)
info$status
```

The wait's overall budget includes its sleeps and status fetches. Each fetch
gets the smaller of the remaining wait budget and its request control.
A cached terminal job returns immediately. Timeout zero means no waiting;
NULL explicitly disables the wait's overall deadline.

A terminal status is not necessarily success: the job may have failed or been
cancelled. Inspect the snapshot instead of treating a return from `wait()` as
proof that every entry succeeded.

Built-in transports should honor remaining I/O budgets. A custom credential
function or transport must cooperate; the library cannot safely preempt
arbitrary user code. A local deadline does not cancel remote work or reverse
charges.

## State whether output retrieval should refresh status

For the usual “tell me what is available now” operation:

```r
entries <- results(job)
```

The default is `status = "refresh"`: fetch status once, update the handle's
snapshot, then retrieve output if the job is terminal. This can make several
HTTP requests, but it never polls.

When your application deliberately trusts an already terminal snapshot:

```r
entries <- results(job, status = "snapshot")
```

That mode makes no new status request. It requires a terminal cached snapshot
before any result fetch and never silently falls back to refreshing. Fetching
can still fail if a remote file expired, disappeared or became inaccessible.
The explicit choice trades a fresher status check for fewer status requests;
it is not a guarantee that cached metadata remains valid forever.

Both forms return typed batch entries in submission order. Keep unsuccessful
entries instead of dropping them and losing alignment with your inputs:

```r
outcomes <- vapply(entries, function(entry) entry$outcome, character(1))
```

A successful entry has a response; an errored entry has an error. Canonical
batch indexes stay zero-based: the first R element `entries[[1]]` has canonical
`index == 0`. An analysis table may add a one-based position, but must not
silently renumber that canonical field.

## Cancellation is not cleanup

```r
cancel(job)
```

This requests remote batch cancellation. It is not what `close()` means, and
is not an automatic consequence of stopping a wait or losing a handle.
There is deliberately no `close(job)` method that secretly cancels remote work.

Reattaching with `batch_job(client, id)` or `video_job(client, id)` explicitly
fetches a status snapshot. It is not merely reconstructing a local value from
an ID. Listing helpers similarly describe their provider requests; public
names are retained even where historical word order is uneven.

## Keep one result distinct from several

| Object | Local observation | Explicit output operation |
|---|---|---|
| Batch job | `snapshot(job)` | `results(job, status = ...)` returns entries |
| Video job | `snapshot(job)` | `result(job, status = ...)` returns a video part |
| Live turn view | `snapshot(view)` | `result(view)` reads to a turn boundary |

These are S3 methods: R chooses the behavior from the kind of object supplied.
They use the shared family words rather than unrelated manual branches.
Type-specific options are checked by the appropriate method;
a `status` option passed to a live turn view is an error, not an ignored field.

Remote video generation stays explicit:

```r
video_client <- new_lm("openai", credential = credential_env("OPENAI_API_KEY"))
video <- video_generate(
  video_client,
  video_generation_request("sora-2", "A sunrise over a quiet lake.")
)
wait(video, timeout = 60)
clip <- result(video, status = "snapshot")
```

The caller decides whether waiting succeeded and what to do with an error or
non-successful status. There is no implicit provider swap, duration change,
input-image omission, or cancellation endpoint invented to make every provider
look identical.

## Cache resources are not response caches

A cached prefix is a stable beginning of a request. A remote cache resource
and a local prefix value are separate things:

```r
prefix <- request(
  "demo-model",
  message_user("Reference material used by later questions.")
)
local_prefix <- cached_prefix(prefix)
next_request <- cached_request(local_prefix, "What is the main point?")
```

These lines build local values. They do not promise a cache hit or a billing
discount. `cache(client, prefix)` may create a remote cache resource where the
selected provider supports one; the name does not make it a pure constructor.
The explicit `cache_create()`, `cache_get()` and related resource operations
keep their existing meanings.

Your application owns cache lifetime and reuse. lm15 preserves the request's
cache intent or refuses it where it cannot be represented; it does not keep a
hidden cache of model answers.
